newsitem.title: UK: Planes grounded as BA hit by strike.
newsitem.headline: Planes grounded as BA hit by strike.

text.p: British Airways was hit by a debilitating strike on Wednesday as cabin crew launched a three-day stoppage that left thousands of passengers stranded.
With up to one in five of its planes grounded, British Airways put on a brave face and said many planes would still fly even as its Heathrow hub faced huge disruption.

Members of the Transport and General Workers' Union (T&G) began the strike at 6.00 a.m. (0500 GMT) despite a warning that strikers would lose perks and face a lockout unless they promised to work normally in the future.
BA, which operates 1,000 flights a day worldwide, said about 100 flights from Heathrow, west of London, were grounded.
"But it's changing by the moment as crew report or not, as the case might be," said BA spokeswoman Terri Urquhart.
"Yesterday about 350 crew reported sick, which was obviously an indication of what's happening. I suspect there will be more sicknesses today," she said.
BBC radio said a fifth of BA flights would not take off.
Pickets carrying banners gathered in the early morning sun near BA's headquarters at Heathrow, while usually frenetic Terminal One was eerily quiet.
As for chances for a breakthrough, both sides expressed some hope of a deal after last-ditch talks between BA managers and union officials, though not in time to stop this stoppage.
BA had hoped to save 42 million pounds ($70.7 million) from its cabin crew operations. The unions oppose the cuts and unless a solution is found, are threatening further 72-hour strikes.
The airline has now suggested that an independent arbiter could examine union proposals for achieving savings.
While the the airline was "very hopeful" of progress, Urquhart said: "As yet, no sign of any movement."
TGWU negotiator George Ryde said he had only seen media reports of the proposal but that it could lead to new talks.
"If we got proper negotiations underway with an objective to secure an agreement, it would avoid any further industrial action," he told BBC television.
British travel agents have been flooded with calls from customers trying to find alternative flights on rival airlines.
BA said its contingency plan, aimed at keeping as many of its flights running as possible, would now swing into action but it admitted thousands of passengers may still be grounded.

Urquhart said the timing of the strike was unfortunate -- the airline last month carried out an expensive facelift aimed at renewing its image -- but that the key to preserving the company's good name was in how it handled the crisis.
"It's obviously upsetting to passengers," she said. "This is disappointing and I think a lot of it depends on how we recover the situation. That's our main focus at the moment."
